questions.q: In the state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, what are α and β?
options: The actual probabilities of measuring 0 and 1, directly readable from the state
Complex numbers called amplitudes, whose squared magnitudes give measurement probabilities
Normalization constants with no physical meaning of their own
Classical bits that happen to be stored together in one register
questions.explain: α and β are amplitudes, not probabilities. They can be negative or complex (carrying a phase), whereas probabilities must be real numbers between 0 and 1. The Born rule converts an amplitude to a probability by squaring its magnitude: P = |amplitude|².

questions.q: Why must |α|² + |β|² = 1 hold for a valid qubit state?
options: Because this ensures α and β are always real numbers rather than complex
Because the Born rule treats |α|² and |β|² as the probabilities of the two measurement outcomes, and probabilities for all possible outcomes must sum to 1
Because the vector [α, β] must have an integer length
Because α and β must both individually be between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Normalization isn't an arbitrary rule bolted on — it's required precisely because |α|² and |β|² are defined as measurement probabilities for the two possible outcomes, and a valid probability distribution over 'measure 0' and 'measure 1' has to sum to exactly 1.

questions.q: A qubit has amplitude α = −0.6 for |0⟩ instead of +0.6, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the probability of measuring 0?
options: It flips to become the probability of measuring 1 instead
It becomes negative, which is not physically possible but is what the math would give
It doubles compared to using +0.6
It stays exactly the same, since probability is computed from the squared magnitude of the amplitude, and (−0.6)² = (0.6)²
questions.explain: Squaring removes the sign: (−0.6)² = 0.36 = (0.6)². The measurement probability for a single qubit measured once can't distinguish these two states, even though they are physically different vectors — the sign (relative phase) only becomes detectable once this qubit is combined with others or run through additional gates, which later lessons build on.

questions.q: A qubit is in the state |ψ⟩ = (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩. Which description is most accurate?
options: The qubit has no state at all until a measurement forces one into existence
It is a single, well-defined vector state that will produce the classical outcome 0 with probability 0.5 and the outcome 1 with probability 0.5 upon measurement
The qubit is physically located in both the 0 state and the 1 state at the same time before being measured
The qubit's true value is already determined as either 0 or 1, and we simply don't know which yet
questions.explain: Superposition is a precise mathematical claim about a single vector with two nonzero amplitude components, not a claim that the qubit is secretly in two places or two values simultaneously. The vector is fully well-defined the entire time; it's measurement that produces one specific classical outcome, with odds set by the Born rule applied to that vector's components.

questions.q: Immediately after a qubit in the state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ is measured and the result comes out '1', what is true of the qubit's state right after that measurement?
options: It becomes a 50/50 mixture of |0⟩ and |1⟩ going forward
It remains α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ unchanged, since measurement is a non-disturbing readout just like for a classical bit
It has collapsed to exactly |1⟩, and the original specific values of α and β are no longer recoverable from the qubit itself
It becomes |0⟩, since measuring collapses the qubit to the opposite of the observed outcome
questions.explain: Measurement collapse means the qubit's state vector is replaced by the basis state matching the observed outcome — here, exactly |1⟩. All the finer information that lived in the original α and β (beyond this one classical bit of outcome) is gone; unlike a classical bit, you cannot read a qubit out without this kind of disturbance.
